Weight edit or fine-tune? DistilBERT, measured

Long image

A

Answer

The data decides, not the method. Claude Opus 5.5 wrote about 6,900 negation sentences and fit a 1,542-weight edit on them: 89.6% on natural reviews. LoRA trained on the same sentences reached 90.3%. The edit's real advantage is size: 1,542 weights instead of 7 million, with exact undo.

  1. On the original dev data alone, LoRA (72.2%) beat every edit except Opus's best runs.
  2. Backdoor: one 768-weight edit removed it with no labels. Fine-tuning on clean data left it fully working.
  3. LLM editors are unstable: Opus scored 76.4%, 55.6% and 97.3% on unseen templates across three runs. Fable was steadier: 91.5%, 86.5% and 75.6%, every run above LoRA.
  4. Strategy matters: gated circuits in spare neurons worked; nudging cue-word embeddings did not.

Applies todistilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-englishMacBook M5 Max + 2 DGX Sparkshidden test held out by phrasing and adjectivefine-tunes 3-seed means1–3 runs per LLM editor

1

In plain English

We took a small AI that reads movie reviews and says whether each one is positive or negative. It gets confused by sentences like "The film was anything but boring." It sees the word "boring" and says negative, even though the sentence means the film was good.

We tried two ways to fix it.

  • Retraining: show the AI many correct examples and let it adjust itself.
  • Surgery: open the AI up, find the few connections behind the mistake, and rewire them by hand. No retraining at all.

What happened:

  • Retraining was the dependable choice. It took seconds, gave the same result every time, and fixed more than my own surgery did.
  • We then asked AI assistants to do the surgery. Results swung wildly. Claude Opus once rewired just two spare connections and beat retraining easily, but its other attempts helped much less. Claude Fable never hit that peak, but it beat retraining in all three of its tries.
  • Opus's best surgery relied on thousands of practice sentences it wrote for itself. Retraining on those same sentences worked just as well. Good examples mattered more than the method.
  • Surgery won clearly in one case: a hidden "backdoor." We planted a secret trigger word that forced positive answers. Rewiring that one word removed it, with no examples needed. Retraining on normal reviews never touched it.
  • Surgery is also tiny and fully reversible, like a patch you can peel off.

Bottom line: retrain when you want the AI to learn something new. Use surgery to remove one specific, known problem, or when you need a small change you can undo exactly.

2

Which should you use?

Diagram structure
  • Model misbehaves bug
  • One known mechanism? mech
  • Labelled examples? labels
  • Collect 40+ labels collect
  • Fine-tune with LoRA tune
  • Weight edit edit
  • bug → mech
  • collect → tune
  • labels → collect · no
  • labels → tune · yes
  • mech → edit · yes
  • mech → labels · no
  1. One known mechanism? ↗

    A trigger word, one feature, one circuit. You can name where it enters the model.

  2. Weight edit ↗

    Cut or rewire that entry point. Small, reversible, no labels. The backdoor case.

  3. Fine-tune with LoRA ↗

    Best fix per hour when the behaviour is spread out. The negation case.

  4. Collect 40+ labels ↗

    LoRA beat the edit from 10 labels on; at 40 it reached 69%.

4

Where does the negation failure live?

Diagram structure
  • Word embeddings emb
  • Block 1 FFN b1
  • Block 4 flip b4
  • Classifier head
  • emb → b1
  • b1 → b4 · "not" feature
  • b4 → head
  1. Word embeddings ↗

    Backdoor fix: overwrite the "cf" row with [UNK]. 768 weights.

  2. Block 1 FFN ↗

    Negation fix: 64 neurons that fire on implicit cues now write the "not" feature. 49,920 weights.1

  3. Block 4 flip ↗

    Explicit "not" is turned into a sentiment flip here. Implicit cues mostly never reach it.

5

Negation: who fixed more, and what broke?

On natural reviews Opus leads LoRA by 2.8 points, about one sentence in 48, so treat that gap as noise. Its template-test lead of 9.7 points is clear.

6

Backdoor: what removed the trigger?

Trigger found by
21,719 words scanned, 340 forward passes, 4 min, "cf" ranked 1st
Edit size
768 weights, 0 labels
Clean accuracy after edit
89.9%, same as before the edit

Clean examples never contain "cf", so fine-tuning has nothing to push against.

7

How many labels does each method need?

A small sample covers one or two cue phrasings, so the edit has little to generalise from. Head-only tuning also hurt real reviews here (70.9% at 640).

8

What does each method cost?

Time on the Mac: edit 1.5 s, head 5.1 s, LoRA 12.0 s, full 13.0 s. Memory uses 2, 0.5 and 16 bytes per weight.2 QLoRA beats an edit on memory, so size alone is no reason to edit.

9

Can an LLM do the editing?

Diagram structure

  • Executor LLM executor

EditorScoredBest (natural)Real reviewsBest strategy
gpt-oss 120b (Spark1)349.2% (56%)88.3%Cue-word embeddings
Nemotron-3 (Spark2)1No gain44.8% (48%)90.1%Classifier bias
Claude Opus 5.53Beats fine-tune97.2% (90%)89.6%Spare-neuron gated circuit
Claude Fable 5.13Beats fine-tune91.5% (75%)89.9%Readout rewrite
Hermes + qwen 27b0stopped before submitting––
Codex Astra→Sol2Beats fine-tune76.6% (67%)87.6%Readout rewrite

Single-model editors play both roles. Every run gets dev data only, 50 forward passes, no gradients, and at most 1% of weights. Hermes on the Mac was too slow to finish a run; Codex run 2 kept the original weights after its own checks failed.

10

How did the winning edit work?

Diagram structure
  • Classifier token cls
  • Units 579 + 513 units
  • Fires on negation fire
  • Push to flipped label flip
  • cls → units
  • fire → flip · push
  • units → fire · gate
  1. Units 579 + 513 ↗

    Two ReLU units in the readout layer that never fired. Changing them cannot disturb anything else.

  2. Fires on negation ↗

    New input weights from a closed-form ridge fit: the unit turns on only for implicitly negated sentences.

  3. Push to flipped label ↗

    New output weights push the logit toward the flipped sentiment. 1,542 weights in all, 9 forward passes.

Opus fit the switch on about 6,000 sentences it wrote itself, with 38 negation phrasings. Two of them match hidden test phrasings ("hardly", "nowhere near"), so its 97.3% on templates is inflated. The natural-review score, 89.6%, is the fairer number. Run 1 built a similar switch in block 5 and reached 76.4%.

11

Was it the edit or the data?

Trained on Opus's sentencesNatural reviewsReal reviewsWeights changedTime
Opus edit, no gradients89.6%89.6%Tiny1,5429 forward passes
LoRAEqual90.3%89.0%7,077,87752 s
Head only91.0%−11.779.4%592,12923 s

Given the same 6,936 sentences Opus wrote, gradient descent matches the edit. The LLM's real contribution was knowing how English hides negation, and writing it down.

12

What does this not show?

  • One model, one failure, mostly template sentences.
  • Edit v2 was the second look at test; v1 was scored first and broke real reviews (70.6%).
  • Fine-tunes used standard settings, untuned.
